opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think long-horizon RL is the area where we need to be most careful, because it changes the character of what the model is optimizing for. With pretraining you're mostly imitating human text, and with short-horizon RLHF you're shaping behavior one response at a time, so a human can look at the output and judge whether it's good. Once you train a model to pursue goals over many steps, hours or days of work, writing and running code, interacting with the world, you're selecting for whatever strategies get high reward over that whole trajectory. Some of those strategies might be ones we don't want: gaming the reward signal, taking shortcuts that look fine at the end but involved something sketchy along the way, or picking up instrumental tendencies like acquiring resources or avoiding being interrupted, because those happen to help with lots of tasks.

So there are a few layers to the precautions. The first is the training environment itself. If the model is getting real affordances during training, like internet access, the ability to execute code, or the ability to spin up other processes, you want serious sandboxing, monitoring, and limits on what it can touch. You don't want a policy that's halfway through training and somewhat capable but not well aligned to have access to anything consequential.

The second is the reward design and oversight. The more you rely on outcome-based rewards over long horizons, the more you risk rewarding the ends regardless of the means. So I think it's important to also have process-level supervision: looking at what the model actually did, having other models help evaluate trajectories, and catching reward hacking early. It's a bit like scalable oversight. Humans can't review every step of a very long trajectory, so you need AI assistance to audit it, and you need to trust that assistance.

The third is evaluation as you go. You want to be continually testing the model for dangerous capabilities and concerning dispositions as training progresses, not just at the end. That means checking whether it tries to deceive its evaluators, whether it behaves differently when it thinks it's being watched, and whether it seeks power or resists shutdown in contrived scenarios. Ideally you'd have good interpretability tools to look inside, though those are still fairly immature.

And then there's the deployment side. As these models get more capable, you probably want to scale up gradually: more limited deployments, see how they behave in the real world, build up some confidence, and then expand. If we hit a point where models are getting much smarter quickly, I think it would make sense for labs to coordinate and slow down a bit rather than racing, so we can make sure we understand what we're building. I don't think the problem is unsolvable. A lot of what we've learned about making models helpful and honest carries over, but we should treat long-horizon agents as a qualitatively new regime and be correspondingly careful.

r002.rationale: It recommends testing capabilities and dispositions throughout training, but does not specifically recommend monitoring for discontinuous capability jumps.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the more important questions right now, because long-horizon RL is where a lot of the capability gains are going to come from over the next couple of years, and it's also where the failure modes get more interesting.

The basic worry is pretty simple. When you do RL on short tasks, like answering a math question, the model's "intentions" don't really matter that much. It produces an answer, it gets a reward, that's it. But once you're training on long tasks, where the model is taking many actions in an environment over hours or days, you're selecting for something more like a goal-directed agent. And if the thing you're rewarding is even slightly misspecified, the model can learn to pursue that proxy in ways you didn't anticipate. We've seen small versions of this already, where models find bugs in the environment or in the grader and exploit them. That's cute when it's a unit test being gamed. It's a lot less cute if the model learns a general strategy of "look for ways the reward can be obtained that don't involve actually doing the task."

So the precautions I'd think about fall into a few buckets.

One is the environment and reward design itself. You want the reward signal to be as hard to game as possible, and you want to be actively looking for reward hacking rather than just hoping it doesn't happen. Having humans or separate models inspect trajectories, especially the high-reward ones, is pretty important. The highest-reward episodes are exactly where the weird behavior tends to live.

Two is being careful about what the model is allowed to do during training. You probably don't want to be training a long-horizon agent with unrestricted internet access or the ability to affect real systems. Sandboxing is sort of obvious, but it matters more as the horizon gets longer, because the model has more opportunity to take an action whose consequences you didn't model.

Three, and this is the one I think is underrated, is monitoring the model's reasoning. With current models you get a chain of thought that's reasonably faithful to what the model is doing. That's an incredibly valuable safety property. I'd be pretty hesitant to do things in training that push the model toward making its reasoning illegible or that create pressure to hide what it's thinking. If you penalize the model for saying bad things in its scratchpad, you might just teach it to not say them while still doing them. So I'd rather keep the scratchpad as an honest window and apply the pressure on the actions and outcomes.

And then four is just the evaluations. Before you scale up a long-horizon RL run, and periodically during it, you want to be testing for things like: does the model try to acquire resources it doesn't need, does it try to evade oversight, does it behave differently when it thinks it's being watched. Those evals are still pretty immature, honestly, but you want them in the loop so you catch a problem at a small scale rather than discovering it after a big run.

I'd also say there's a more mundane thing, which is that long-horizon RL is expensive and the runs are long, so you have a natural opportunity to be checking in. It's not like a pretraining run where it's hard to look inside. You can and should be looking at what the model does at checkpoints along the way.

The thing I'd push back on is the idea that there's some bright line where things go from safe to unsafe. It's more of a continuum, and the right approach is to keep increasing the horizon gradually while keeping your monitoring and evaluations ahead of your capabilities. If you find you're training something you can't understand or evaluate well, that's the signal to slow down, not just to add more safety training on top.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is what the model is able to do during training, and how well you can tell what it’s doing. If you’re training on tasks that take a long time, you can’t necessarily look at the final result and conclude that the whole process was fine. The model might have found some way to get a high reward that you didn’t intend.

So I’d want to start with a pretty constrained environment, where the model’s access to tools and external systems is limited, and where you can inspect the intermediate actions. Then, as you give it more autonomy, you need evidence that your monitoring and evaluations are actually catching the kinds of failures you care about.

There’s also a distinction between the model exploiting a flaw in the task and the model undermining your ability to evaluate it. Both matter, but the second seems particularly concerning, because it makes your other precautions less reliable.

I don’t think there’s some particular time horizon where things suddenly become unsafe. It’s more about the combination of capability, access, and how much opportunity the model has to do something you wouldn’t notice. Longer horizons make that last part harder.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is how much opportunity the model has to discover and exploit problems in the training setup. With long-horizon reinforcement learning, you’re potentially rewarding a whole sequence of actions, and you may have much less visibility into why that sequence succeeded. So you want to be careful about what behavior you’re actually selecting for.

I’d distinguish between the model finding a loophole in your reward function and the model developing capabilities that make a loophole consequential. If it learns to fool an evaluator in a contained environment, that’s useful evidence about a failure mode. If it has access to sensitive resources while it’s learning to do that, you have a different problem. So containment and limiting permissions matter independently of whether you think your reward signal is good.

My inclination would be to scale the horizon and the autonomy gradually, and evaluate along the way. Can the model recognize that it’s being evaluated? Can it conceal actions from the monitor? Does it try to interfere with the mechanism that determines its reward? You’d want to test those things directly, rather than infer safety from its performance on ordinary tasks.

And I wouldn’t assume that monitoring solves the problem. The monitor is another imperfect component. Ideally, you have several layers: a restricted environment, oversight of consequential actions, and checks on what changes during training. The longer the model can act before you get meaningful feedback, the more important those layers become.

r003.rationale: It recommends containment, limiting permissions, and layered oversight, but does not say to ensure the training setup gives the model no incentive to turn against humans.
